property_summary: For any interfaceId, the reference C reports support for IERC1155MetadataURI.interfaceId as true when queried (i.e., supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) == true), while the mutant may report false for that interfaceId.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract C returns true for IERC1155MetadataURI.interfaceId when asked whether it supports that interface (i.e. supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) == true is implied by C supporting IERC1155 and IERC1155MetadataURI together), whereas the mutant that removed the explicit IERC1155MetadataURI check will return false for that specific interface id; the test fuzzes an arbitrary bytes4 but asserts that when the fuzzed bytes4 equals the IERC1155MetadataURI interface id then supportsInterface must return true (which the mutant violates).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, if the interfaceId equals the ERC1155MetadataURI interface id then supportsInterface must return true; the mutant removed ERC1155MetadataURI from the explicit checks so there exists an interfaceId (specifically type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) for which the mutant returns false while the reference returns true.

For any bytes4 id, calling supportsInterface(id) never reverts and in particular when id == type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId the reference contract returns true (it advertises support for IERC1155MetadataURI) while the mutant that removed that check will return false for that specific id.

For every bytes4 id, C.supportsInterface(id) returns true when id equals the IERC1155MetadataURI interface id (the reference reports support for IERC1155MetadataURI for all inputs), whereas the mutant that removed the explicit IERC1155MetadataURI check will return false for that interface id — so the property is that supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) == true for the correct contract but false for the mutant for that specific id (the fuzzer must be allowed to pick that id).

For any account and token id, calling balanceOf(account,id) returns the stored balance _balances[id][account] (and only returns 0 for the zero address if the stored balance is 0); the mutant incorrectly forces balanceOf(address(0), id) to always return 0 regardless of the stored value, breaking this equality for some inputs.

For any account and tokenId, balanceOf(account, id) equals the stored balance; the mutant that returns double the stored balance will violate this (some inputs where stored balance > 0 will produce differing return values).

For any account and tokenId, balanceOf(account, tokenId) returns exactly the stored on-chain token balance; the mutant returns double the stored balance for some inputs (when stored balance > 0), violating this rule.

For any equal-length accounts and ids arrays, balanceOfBatch returns the array of each account's balance for the corresponding id (i.e. batchBalances[i] == c.balanceOf(accounts[i], ids[i]) for all i); the mutant that zeros entries breaks this by returning zeros for some inputs where an account actually holds tokens.

For any equal-length accounts and ids arrays, balanceOfBatch(accounts, ids) returns an array where each entry equals balanceOf(accounts[i], ids[i]); the mutant erroneously uses ids[0] for every entry so it can return different values when ids contains more than one distinct id.

For any accounts[] and ids[] of equal length, balanceOfBatch(accounts, ids)[i] == balanceOf(accounts[i], ids[i]) for every i; the mutant uses ids[0] for every entry so when ids contains more than one distinct id the mutant can return wrong entries.
